name: Surgical Technologist
description: Surgical technologists build and defend the sterile field in an operating theatre — setting up instruments and equipment, scrubbing in with the surgical team, passing instruments through the case, and counting every sponge and needle before the patient is closed. ⚠ A median of $64,650, usually reached through a certificate rather than a degree. ⚠⚠⚠ And this is the one health credential on this site that FLORIDA DOES NOT REGULATE — no licence, no board, no state gate — which makes checking your programme's accreditation entirely your job. Several commercial sites say otherwise; they are wrong, and this page shows why.
credentialNote: ⚠⚠⚠ Florida does NOT license or register surgical technologists. There is no board, no state examination and no state credential. Chapter 468 of the Florida Statutes, which regulates most allied-health professions, runs to Part XVI and contains no part for surgical technology. ⚠⚠ A 2022 bill, SB 1828, would have created Part XVII — Surgical Technology and Central Service Technician Services — and set employment conditions including an accredited programme and national certification. It DIED IN THE SENATE HEALTH POLICY COMMITTEE on 14 March 2022 and never became law. ⚠ Several commercial career-advice sites state as current fact that Florida requires certification within twelve months of graduation. That describes the bill, not the law. ⚠⚠ What binds instead is the EMPLOYER: hospitals and ambulatory surgery centres set their own credentialing, and the industry standard is the Certified Surgical Technologist (CST) awarded by the NBSTSA, which requires graduation from a programme accredited by CAAHEP or ABHES. Because there is no state gate, a non-accredited programme will not be caught by anyone but you — verify the accreditation directly with the accreditor before you pay a deposit.
bodyHtml:
What the work actually is

O*NET, on surgical technologists: maintain a proper sterile field during surgical procedures; count sponges, needles, and instruments before and after operation; hand instruments and supplies to surgeons and surgeons' assistants, hold retractors and cut sutures; scrub arms and hands and assist the surgical team to scrub and put on gloves, masks, and surgical clothing; wash and sterilize equipment, using germicides and sterilizers.

⚠ The count is not administrative detail — it is the job. A retained sponge or needle is a never-event, and the technologist is the person whose count stands between the patient and one. So is the sterile field: you are the member of the team whose whole attention is on whether it has been broken.

⚠⚠ You also have to know the case. A good scrub has the next instrument in the surgeon's hand before it is asked for, which means knowing the steps of the procedure and where this one has got to. That is why the programmes are organised around surgical specialties rather than around subjects.

Projected need and wages

✅ O*NET and the BLS agree closely here.

  • O*NET (2024–34): 115,600 employed, growth faster than average (5% to 6%), 7,000 openings a year, median $64,650 (2025).
  • BLS OOH (2025–35): 142,800 jobs, growth 5%, faster than average, +7,400, median $64,700, entry a postsecondary nondegree award.

⚠ And there is a level above it worth knowing about from the start. The BLS reports surgical assistants — also called surgical first assistants, who make incisions, place clamps and close — at a $66,800 median. It is a further credential rather than a promotion you drift into, and it is the obvious progression for a technologist who wants more of the operation.

⚠⚠⚠ Florida does not regulate this job, and the internet will tell you it does

Every other health path on this site ends at a state licence. This one does not. Florida has no board of surgical technology, no state examination and no registration. Chapter 468 of the Florida Statutes — speech-language pathology, occupational therapy, radiological personnel, respiratory therapy, athletic trainers, and a dozen more — runs to Part XVI and stops. There is no part for surgical technology.

⚠⚠ A bill would have changed that and did not pass. SB 1828 of 2022, Surgical Technology and Central Service Technician Services, would have created Part XVII and set conditions on who a health care facility could employ. Its last action reads “3/14/2022 Senate — Died in Health Policy”.

⚠⚠⚠ Several commercial “how to become a surgical tech in Florida” sites state, as current law, that you must obtain national certification within twelve months of graduating. That is a description of the failed bill. It is not the law, and you should not plan around it — nor should you assume the state is checking anything on your behalf.

⚠⚠ So the accreditation check is entirely yours

In respiratory therapy, paramedicine or dental hygiene, a programme that is not accredited cannot get its graduates licensed, so the state effectively polices programme quality. Here there is no such backstop. What employers ask for is the CST from the NBSTSA, and eligibility for that examination runs through a programme accredited by CAAHEP or ABHES.

⚠ Ask the programme for its accreditor and its programme number, then check it on the accreditor's own site rather than the college's. Ask also for the CST first-attempt pass rate. Accredited programmes report it; a programme that will not give you a number is telling you something.

⚠⚠ Two delivery routes, and only one builds toward a degree

As in emergency medical services, Florida runs the same training two ways and does not flag the difference at enrolment:

RouteShapeWhat you get
College credit — STS 1302 and the 2000-level coursesa certificate or an associate degree✅ credit that counts toward a degree later
⚠ PSAV clock hours — STS 0010, 0011, 0012about 1,030 hours in three occupational completion pointsa certificate carrying no college credit

⚠ Ten institutions carry each of the three clock-hour courses, so this is not a fringe route — it is how much of the state teaches the subject, and it is usually faster and cheaper. It is a perfectly good way into the operating theatre. It is a poor way in if you may later want an associate degree, a bachelor's, or the nursing route, because none of those hours transfer.

⚠⚠ And there is a shorter exit worth knowing about: STS 0015 Central Supply Technician, about 210 clock hours, at 10 institutions. Sterile processing is the department that decontaminates, inspects and sterilises every instrument set the theatre uses. It is a real job in its own right, it is a common way to see the environment before committing to the full programme, and it is the credential the failed 2022 bill would also have covered.

⚠ The numbers do not travel well

Florida carries 96 surgical technology course numbers across 27 public institutions, and the most widely shared reaches only 11 — the introductory course. Almost half the numbers are carried by a single college. The same subject appears as Surgical Procedures I, Surgical Specialties & Procedures I and Surgical Technique & Procedures, under STS 1323, STS 2323, STS 2323C and STS 1177C.

⚠⚠ Treat these programmes as one-college packages. Take general education and the sciences wherever suits you; take the surgical sequence in one place, and expect to repeat rather than transfer if you move mid-programme.

Necessary skills

  • Sterile discipline that does not lapse when you are tired. The field is either sterile or it is not, and nobody else is watching it as closely as you are.
  • Anticipation. Knowing the steps of the procedure well enough to have the instrument ready, not to fetch it when asked.
  • Counting, reliably, under pressure and interruption. This is a genuine skill and it is examined as one.
  • Standing still for hours. Long cases are long, and you cannot leave the field. This is the part most students underestimate.
  • Composure with surgeons. Theatres run on hierarchy and speed, and being spoken to sharply mid-case is normal rather than personal.

Advice

⚠⚠ Verify CAAHEP or ABHES accreditation yourself, with the accreditor. On every other health path the state would catch an unaccredited programme for you. Here nothing does, which makes this the single most consequential five minutes of your research.

⚠ Decide the credit question before you enrol, not after. If there is any chance of a degree later — and the route to perioperative nursing or to surgical first assisting usually needs one — take the college-credit route even though the clock-hour one is quicker.

⚠ Consider central sterile processing first if you are unsure. Around 210 hours, ten institutions, and it puts you inside the department that supplies the theatre. It is much cheaper than discovering in month six that you cannot stand the room.

And ask to observe a full case before you commit. Not a video — a real list, start to finish. The work is remarkable and it is not for everyone, and four hours in a corner of a theatre will tell you which you are.

programs.note: The programme itself — 25 Florida public institutions, mostly certificates, with technical colleges carrying a large share. ⚠ Read its degrees note before enrolling: the clock-hour route is about 1,030 hours and carries no college credit, and there is no state licence to catch an unaccredited programme.

⚠ Not a route from here — the surgical technology credential gives no advanced standing, and you would start a nursing programme from the beginning. Named because a perioperative RN is the level above you in the same room, with assessment, charge and management roles that are closed to a technologist, and because it is the move many technologists eventually make.

⚠ Not a route here. Named as the closest structural comparison: another certificate-first acute-care credential taught heavily at technical colleges, at similar pay. ⚠⚠ The difference is environment rather than difficulty — EMS is unscheduled and outdoors, this is a scheduled list in one controlled room.

courses.reason: Anatomy and Physiology I — 20 institutions. Required with a grade of C or higher, and the course that makes the anatomy of a procedure legible rather than memorised.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ Two equivalent packagings: 20 institutions split it into BSC2085 plus BSC2085L, and 7 carry the combined BSC2085C. Where it is split, take both halves in the same term.

courses.reason: Anatomy and Physiology I Laboratory — 19 institutions, the corequisite half.
Anatomy and Physiology II — 19 institutions. Required alongside the first half by the associate-degree route, unlike several other health programmes on this site that name only one.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ Also carried as the combined BSC2086C at 7 institutions.

courses.reason: Anatomy and Physiology II Laboratory — 19 institutions.
Microbiology — 16 institutions. The science behind the sterile field: what you are excluding, how it gets in, and why the sterilisation parameters are what they are.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ Required with a grade of C or higher at Indian River, and paired with MCB2010L (15 institutions).

courses.reason: Microbiology Laboratory — 15 institutions, the corequisite half, where aseptic technique is practised rather than described.
Medical Terminology — 8 institutions. Required outright, and the language every preference card, instrument name and operative note is written in.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ Florida numbers this subject twice: HSC2531 at 8 institutions and HSC1531 at 16. Indian River's surgical technology A.S. names HSC2531 specifically — take the one your own catalogue lists.

courses.reason: Introduction to Psychology — 33 institutions. Required by the associate-degree route, and more useful than it sounds in a room that runs on hierarchy, stress and communication under time pressure.
English Composition I — 39 institutions, in the general-education core of the associate-degree route.

Introduction to Surgical Technology — 11 institutions, the most widely carried course in the prefix. The role, the sterile field, aseptic technique, theatre layout and the legal and ethical framework.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ Also carried as STS1302C, STS1302L and STS1303 Fundamentals of Surgical Technology at other colleges. This prefix names the same subjects differently at nearly every institution.

courses.reason: Operating Room Technique I, Instrumentation — 5 institutions. Identifying, handling, assembling and caring for instrument sets, which is the craft the job is built on.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ Also taught as STS1304L Operating Room Technique II and STS1327L Principles and Practices of Surgical Technology Laboratory at other colleges.

courses.reason: Perioperative Patient Care Concepts — 5 institutions. Positioning, skin preparation, draping, catheterisation and monitoring: what happens to the patient before the first incision.
Pharmacology and Anesthesia — 6 institutions. Medications on the sterile field, their labelling and handling, and what the anaesthetist is doing at the head of the table.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ Also carried as STS1340C at 5 institutions, titled Surgical Science and Pharmacology at some colleges. ⚠⚠ Drug handling on the field is a common source of error and is examined closely.

courses.reason: Surgical Procedures I — 6 institutions. The specialty-by-specialty core: general, obstetric and gynaecological, genitourinary and ear, nose and throat procedures, step by step.
courses.variantNote: ⚠⚠ The same subject appears as STS1323, STS2323, STS2323C, STS2323L and STS1177C across the state. ⚠ Check which your college uses before comparing programmes or planning a transfer.

courses.reason: Surgical Procedures II — 10 institutions, the second most widely carried course. Orthopaedic, cardiothoracic, vascular, neurological and ophthalmic procedures.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ Also carried as STS2324L and STS2324C. ⚠⚠ This is where the specialties that pay best later are introduced — cardiothoracic and neurosurgery scrub roles are the usual route to a higher wage.

courses.reason: Professional Skills for the Operating Room Team — 7 institutions. Team roles, communication protocols, the surgical safety checklist and the counting procedure as a formal process.
Surgical Clinical I — 7 institutions. The first supervised placement, scrubbing cases in a hospital theatre under a preceptor.
courses.variantNote: ⚠⚠ A clinical course: full theatre shifts on the hospital's schedule, commonly starting before seven in the morning, at whichever facility your college has an affiliation with. Expect background screening, immunisations, TB screening, drug screening and current BLS to be complete BEFORE the first day.

courses.reason: Surgical Clinical II — 7 institutions, the terminal placement. Its case log is what an employer asks for, and what the CST examination assumes you have scrubbed.
courses.variantNote: ⚠⚠ Keep the case log. Accredited programmes set a minimum number of cases by specialty and role, and it is the only record of what you actually did — the transcript line will not say.

courses.reason: Surgical Technologist, first occupational completion point — 10 institutions, 343 clock hours. The PSAV route, and how much of Florida actually teaches this subject.
courses.variantNote: ⚠⚠⚠ Measured in CLOCK HOURS and carrying NO college credit. With STS0011 and STS0012 it runs to about 1,030 hours and reaches the same CST examination as the credit route. ⚠ It is faster and cheaper and a legitimate way in — but none of it transfers if you later want a degree, and nobody points that out at enrolment.

courses.reason: Central Supply Technician — 10 institutions, 210 clock hours. Sterile processing: decontamination, inspection, assembly and sterilisation of every instrument set the theatre uses.
courses.variantNote: ⚠ A separate and much shorter credential, and a good way to see the environment before committing to the full programme. ⚠⚠ It is also a real destination — central sterile departments hire and promote — and it was the other occupation the failed 2022 bill would have covered.

There is no Florida licence, board or registration for this occupation.

Gulf Coast State 43, Santa Fe 37, FSCJ 26, Sheridan Technical 24, Orange Technical 20. ⚠ Technical colleges produce roughly a third of the state's graduates.

sources.note: The worked Florida curriculum behind this page's course list: a 44-credit major requiring both halves of anatomy and physiology, microbiology with its laboratory, medical terminology (HSC2531) and psychology, with a grade of C or higher required in medical terminology, microbiology and every STS course.
